Seoul by ground elevation: darker is higher

STA3115 EXPLORATORY DATA ANALYSIS, FINAL PROJECT

Where do all the Ddareungi go?

Bikes roll downhill,
and nobody rides them back up

Group 1, November 26, 2026

Hello, we are Group 1. Our topic is Ddareungi, Seoul’s public bike system. We asked a simple question: where do all the bikes go? The short answer is in the title. In the morning, bikes roll downhill, and nobody rides them back up.

WHAT IS DDAREUNGI

Seoul’s public bike: rent at one station, return at any other

45,000 bikes

at about 2,800 stations (2025)

Since 2015

5.06 million members and 250 million rides in ten years

Rent

Scan the QR code on the bike in the app and the lock opens. Open to anyone 13 or older, around the clock.

Return

Lock the back wheel at any station and the return is logged. Outside a station, the rental keeps running.

Price

A day pass costs 1,000 won per hour. Season passes cover 7 to 365 days; when time runs out, return and rent again.

Commute

The commute hours, 7–9 am and 5–7 pm, carry 44% of weekday rides. The city already sends 33 staff to 330 stations that run too full or too empty.

Photos: *Youngjin, CC BY-SA 3.0 (left); Sarang, public domain (right); Wikimedia Commons. Facts: Seoul Metropolitan Government, 2024 and 2025.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

First, a quick introduction for anyone who has not used Ddareungi. It started in October 2015, and today about 45,000 bikes are spread over some 2,800 stations. You rent a bike with an app: scan the QR code and the lock opens. You can return it at any station by locking the back wheel. A day pass costs 1,000 won an hour, and season passes are also available. The key point for us: on weekdays, the morning and evening commute hours account for 44% of all rides. Because people pick up a bike at one station and leave it at another, some stations run empty while others overflow. The city knows this already. At commute times it sends 33 staff to 330 stations that are too full or too empty. That imbalance is what we studied.

WHY THIS MATTERS

Rides are falling while the deficit grows

44.9M → 37.4M

rides a year from 2023 to 2025, with −14.8% in 2025 alone

₩17.6 bn

operating deficit in 2025, nearly twice the ₩9.4 bn of 2022

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Ddareungi grew quickly, from 32 million rides in 2021 to almost 45 million in 2023. Since then it has fallen two years in a row, to 37.4 million in 2025, a drop of 14.8% in one year. Over the same period the operating deficit grew, from 9.4 billion won in 2022 to 17.6 billion won in 2025, nearly twice as much.

WHERE THE MONEY GOES

Over half the operating cost goes to moving bikes around

53%

of the operating cost goes to redistributing bikes

Our question

Where do bikes pile up, where do they run out, and why?

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Where does the money go? According to Bike Magazine, 53% of the operating cost is staff time spent redistributing bikes. That is the work of the trucks you see on the street, picking up bikes at one station and dropping them off at another. They are needed because some stations run dry while others overflow. So our question is: where do bikes pile up, where do they run out, and why? If the data can answer that, trucks can be sent to the right place at the right time.

What might matter

1

Time of day

2

Weather

3

Elevation and slope

4

Distance to the nearest subway station

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Before looking at the data, we listed what might decide where a bike ends up. Time of day, because commuting and leisure trips look different. Weather: rain and temperature. Terrain, because pedalling uphill is hard. And transit, since many people ride to and from the subway. The first two tell us which days to study; the last two are possible explanations.

STEP 1. CHOOSING THE DAYS

Weekdays follow a clear commute pattern; weekends do not

8 am, 6 pm

two sharp weekday peaks, with 11,300 and 13,200 rides in the hour

One broad peak

on weekends and holidays, highest at 5 pm with 6,900 rides

Weekdays only

from here on, with the 7–9 am commute as the key window

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

First, time of day. This chart shows the average number of rides started in each hour. On weekdays there are two sharp peaks, at 8 in the morning and 6 in the evening: that is commuting. On weekends and holidays there is a single broad peak in the afternoon. Because the weekday pattern repeats day after day, we focus on weekdays, and especially on the morning commute, from 7 to 9 am.

STEP 1. CHOOSING THE DAYS

Rainy days are too irregular to model, so we set them aside

Dry days

follow a smooth curve: rides rise with temperature and dip in the hottest weeks (LOESS, span 0.75)

Each dot is one weekday: 480 in all, every Monday to Friday in 2024 and 2025 except public holidays (490), minus 10 days with mismatched records.

Rainy days

(1 mm or more) scatter far from any curve

3×

larger residual spread on rainy days (SD 37k vs 13k rides), and it grows with temperature

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Next, weather. Each dot is one weekday, with temperature across and total rides up. On dry days the points follow a smooth LOESS curve: rides rise with temperature and dip a little in the hottest weeks. On days with 1 millimetre of rain or more, rides fall and the points scatter. The residuals make this clear: on dry days they are small and even, with a standard deviation of about 13,000 rides. On rainy days the spread is three times larger and grows with temperature. So the effect of rain depends on things our data does not capture, such as when and how hard it rains. That is why we set rainy days aside and keep dry weekdays.

STEP 2. WHAT WE MEASURE

378 dry weekdays, 2,843 stations, every trip

Net outflow

Rentals minus returns at a station. Positive means the station loses bikes; negative means it gains them.

Computed for the whole day and for the 7–9 am commute, and divided by the number of docks so that large and small stations can be compared.

Data

Every station-to-station trip in 2024–2025 (Seoul Open Data, 5-minute records), hourly KMA weather, station elevation from 1:5,000 contour maps, subway stations and land-use zones.

A dry weekday is a weekday that is not a public holiday and has under 1 mm of rain. We dropped ten days on which rentals and returns did not match.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

That leaves 378 dry weekdays in 2024 and 2025, and 2,843 stations. Our measure is net outflow: rentals minus returns. When it is positive, the station loses bikes; when it is negative, it gains them. We compute it for the whole day and for the morning commute, and divide it by the number of docks so that large and small stations can be compared. A daily net outflow of plus 40% means a station loses bikes equal to 40% of its docks every day, and a truck has to bring them back.

STEP 3. WHERE

Each morning, some districts empty out while others fill up

8 am, 6 pm

every district is busiest at the two commute peaks

Losing, 7–9 am

Gwangjin +27%, Seodaemun +23%, Dongdaemun +18% of docks

Gaining, 7–9 am

Seongdong −39%, Jung −15%, Yeongdeungpo −13%: the office areas of Seongsu, the city centre and Yeouido

Over the whole day the colours do not cancel out. What is left over is what the trucks have to move.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Now, where. First, plain use: rentals per station in each hour. Drag the slider and you can see every district peak at 8 am and 6 pm. Next, net flow during the morning commute. Red districts lose bikes and blue districts gain them. Gwangjin, Seodaemun and Dongdaemun lose bikes, while the office areas of Seongdong, the city centre and Yeouido gain them. Over the whole day the colours do not cancel out, and what is left over is exactly what the trucks have to move. But a district is a large unit. What is it about a station that makes it lose bikes?

STEP 4. WHY

Of the station features we tested, elevation matters most

Outcome: daily net outflow (% of docks), 2,843 stations. ρ: Spearman correlation, one feature at a time. β: all five features in one linear model on standardised variables (R² = 0.15). The model ranks the features; it is not meant to predict.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

To see which station features go with losing bikes, we compared five candidates. The first column is the rank correlation with daily net outflow, one feature at a time. The second is the coefficient when all five enter one linear model on a standardised scale. Elevation comes first on both: a correlation of 0.40 and a coefficient of 0.33, three times larger than any other. Distance to the subway and land-use zone hardly matter. The model explains only 15% of the variation, so we use it to rank the features, not to predict. Let us look at elevation directly.

STEP 4. WHY

The higher the station, the more bikes it loses

Every one of the 143 stations at 50 m or higher loses bikes.

Hover over a dot to name the station.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

This is our core figure. Each dot is a station, with elevation across and daily net outflow up, as a share of its docks. Below 20 metres, stations gain bikes on average, 15% of their docks a day. Between 20 and 40 metres they are roughly balanced. At 40 metres and above, they lose 42% of their docks every day, and 91% of them end the day short. Every one of the 143 stations above 50 metres loses bikes. The red LOESS curve sits just below zero on low ground, crosses zero at about 25 metres and reaches around plus 50% by 60 metres. We stop the curve at 80 metres, where there are too few stations.

STEP 4. WHY

On the map, the stations that lose bikes sit on the hills

Share of stations that end the day short of bikes, by station elevation

Red on the hills
The northern foothills (Eunpyeong, Gangbuk, Dobong), Gwanak, and the hills of Seodaemun, Seongbuk and Jongno.

Blue in the valleys
Along the Han River and its streams, Yeouido, Seongsu and Gangnam’s main roads.

Shaded: ground 50 m or higher. Terrain and contours: Seoul 1:5,000 digital topographic map.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Here is the same pattern on the map. First, the terrain: the shaded areas are ground 50 metres or higher. Now we add the stations that lose more than 10% of their docks every day, in red. They sit on the shaded hills: the northern foothills, Gwanak, and the hills of Seodaemun, Seongbuk and Jongno. The bars on the right say the same with numbers: below 15 metres, 39% of stations end the day short; at 50 metres and above, every one of them does. Finally, the stations that gain bikes, in blue, line the Han River, its streams and the flat business areas. So elevation matters. The next question is how. Where do the bikes go?

STEP 5. HOW

Bikes flow downhill: people ride down but rarely ride back up

Arrows

net flow out of each 1 km cell

69% downhill

of net flow on sloping ground, against 7% uphill (morning: 59% vs 12%)

1% uphill

of the 120 largest flows in the hills of Seodaemun, Jongno and Seongbuk

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

To see how, we turned every trip into a flow map. For each pair of places we take the trips from A to B minus the trips from B to A, and sum them into one arrow per square kilometre, drawn over the terrain. Darker ground is higher. Then we colour each arrow by whether it points downhill or uphill. On sloping ground, 69% of the net flow runs downhill and only 7% uphill. Zoom in on Seodaemun, Jongno and Seongbuk, which combine hills and many commuters: of the 120 largest net flows between neighbourhoods, 58% run downhill and just 1% uphill. People ride down and make the trip back some other way, so the bikes stay at the bottom.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR THE TRUCKS

Does every hill-top station need a truck every morning?

?

Many stations are emptied during the 7–9 am commute.

?

But if residents ride back in the evening, the station refills by night and needs no truck.

→

So we ask two questions of every station: is it emptied in the morning, and is it still short at night?

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

What does this mean for the trucks? Should a truck rush to every station that is emptied in the morning? Not necessarily. If residents ride back home in the evening, the station refills by night and needs no truck. We call this the self-balancing hypothesis. To test it, we ask two questions of every station: is it emptied in the morning, and is it still short at the end of the day?

STEP 6. WHICH STATIONS NEED A TRUCK

Two questions sort the stations into four groups

2 questions

emptied 7–9 am? still short at night? (net outflow beyond ±10% of docks)

2,843

stations, each sorted by its two answers

893 vs 703

G1 stays short and needs a truck; G2 refills by night and does not

1,596

stations are emptied in the morning. Why does only half of them recover?

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Here are the two questions as a grid. The columns ask whether a station is emptied during the morning commute; the rows ask whether it is still short at the end of the day. Stations within 10% of their docks on both counts are balanced. Top right is G1, which stays short: 893 stations, 31%. Bottom right is G2, which refills by night: 703. Bottom left is G3, which collects bikes all day, and top left is G4, an office hub that fills in the morning and empties during the day. Each tile also shows a typical day for its group: up means bikes leave, down means bikes arrive. Now look at the right column: 1,596 stations lose bikes every morning. About half of them get their bikes back by night, and the other half never do. Why?

STEP 6. WHICH STATIONS NEED A TRUCK

Each group occupies its own part of the city

G1 Stays short

893 stations, 31%: across the city, densest on hillsides

G2 Refills by night

703, 25%: flat residential areas

G3 Collects bikes

533, 19%: along streams and on low ground

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

On the map, each group occupies its own part of the city. G1, which stays short, sits on the hills: the northern foothills, Gwanak, Seodaemun and Eunpyeong. In Seodaemun, 60% of the stations that are not balanced are G1, the highest share of any district. G2, which refills by night, is found in flat residential areas such as Nowon, Gangdong and Songpa. G3, which collects bikes, lines the streams: Jungnangcheon, Anyangcheon and Tancheon. G4 sits in the business districts: Yeouido, Gwanghwamun and the Guro Digital Complex.

STEP 6. WHICH STATIONS NEED A TRUCK

Same morning, different evening: the difference is the hill

−5.7 bikes

net return to a G2 station in the evening commute, 5–8 pm

−1.3 bikes

net return to a G1 station: few people ride back up

28 m vs 19 m

median elevation of G1 and G2; distance to the subway is similar (500 m vs 470 m)

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

To see why, we compare the two groups hour by hour. G2, in orange: bikes leave in the morning and the evening commute brings them back, so by night the station is full again. G1, in red: the same morning drain, but only a trickle comes back in the evening, about 1.3 bikes per station against 5.7 for G2. What separates them? Elevation. G1 stations sit at a median of 28 metres, G2 stations at 19. Distance to the subway is almost the same, 500 against 470 metres. People ride down to the station in the morning, and in the evening few of them ride back up the hill.

STEP 7. WHEN

The hills are refilled every day, but not before the morning rush

−4.4

bikes a day that riders take from stations at 40 m and above

+4.4

bikes a day returned there by other moves, mostly trucks

0.99

correlation of stock change with rides at 7–9 am: almost no refilling in the peak

28%

of commute hours in which those stations have no bikes

2025 dry weekdays; hourly stock matched with trips.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Trip records do not show the trucks. So we also took the hourly stock at every station and matched it with the trips: whatever the rides do not explain is other moves, mostly trucks. Below 20 metres, riders bring in about one bike a day and other moves take about one away. At 40 metres and above, riders take away about four bikes a day and other moves bring almost exactly four back. So trucks already go up the hills every day. But between 7 and 9 am, stock moves almost exactly with the rides, a correlation of 0.99. Almost nothing is refilled during the peak, and those hill-top stations still have no bikes in 28% of commute hours. The question is not only where the trucks go, but when.

CONCLUSION

Get bikes up the hills before the morning rush, and leave alone the stations that refill themselves

Bikes roll downhill in the morning and are not ridden back up: 69% of net flow on sloping ground runs downhill.

An empty station at 9 am is not always a problem: 703 stations (G2) refill on their own by night.

The hills are refilled every day, yet stay empty in 28% of commute hours, because the refill does not come before the rush.

Refill the 893 hill-top G1 stations before 7 am, using bikes from the 533 low-lying G3 stations. And do not merge stations on ride counts alone: half of the hill-top merge candidates are already empty in the morning.

To sum up. Bikes roll downhill in the morning and are not ridden back up. Because of that, an empty station at 9 am is not always a problem: 703 stations get their bikes back by night without any help. The stations that really need a truck are the 893 G1 stations on the hills, and they are already refilled every day, just not before the morning rush. So the plan is about timing: take bikes from the 533 G3 stations on low ground, which collect bikes all day, and have them on the hills before 7 am. One more point for the debate about cutting the system: if you merge the least-used stations on ride counts alone, half of the hill-top candidates are stations that are already empty in the morning. Their low use may mean no bikes, not no demand.

LIMITS

What this analysis cannot tell us

1

Trucks are visible only as stock changes that rides do not explain, so we cannot tell when each truck arrives.

2

An empty station records no rentals, so demand on the hills is probably higher than we see.

3

We looked only at dry weekdays; weekends and rainy days need their own analysis.

4

We describe patterns; we do not estimate how much a new truck schedule would save.

STA3115 Exploratory Data Analysis, Group 1

Some limits. First, we see the trucks only indirectly, as the change in stock that rides do not explain, so we cannot tell when each truck arrives. Second, an empty station records no rentals, so demand on the hills is probably higher than our numbers show. Third, we looked only at dry weekdays. And fourth, this is an exploratory study: we describe the pattern, but we do not estimate how much a new truck schedule would save.
